Identiﬁcation of Novel Noninvasive Markers for
Diagnosing Nonalcoholic Steatohepatitis and Related
Fibrosis by Data Mining
Keito Yoshimura,1* Takeshi Okanoue,2* Hayao Ebise,1* Tsuyoshi Iwasaki,1 Masayuki Mizuno,2
Toshihide Shima,2 Junji Ichihara,1 and Kazuto Yamazaki1
It is important that patients with nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) are diagnosed
and treated early to prevent serious complications, such as liver cirrhosis or hepatocellu-
lar carcinoma. However, current methods for NASH diagnosis are invasive given that
they rely on liver biopsy, making early diagnosis difﬁcult. In this study, we developed
novel noninvasive markers for the diagnosis of NASH and NASH-related ﬁbrosis. A
total of 132 Japanese patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease were included in this
study. Blood samples were collected, and 261 biomolecules were quantiﬁed in serum.
Using cluster and pathway analyses, we identiﬁed biomolecule modules connected to
biological events that occur with disease progression to NASH. The modules were used
as variables for diagnosis, leading to a NASH diagnostic marker associated with two
biological events, that is, protective response to hepatic steatosis and hepatitis-causing
innate immune response. Regarding the NASH-related ﬁbrosis marker, immunological
responses to hepatocyte injury were identiﬁed as a biological event. To develop diagnos-
tic markers for NASH and NASH-related ﬁbrosis, speciﬁc biomolecules were selected
from each biomolecule module. The former marker was obtained by averaging the levels
of four biomolecules, whereas the latter was obtained by averaging the levels of two bio-
molecules. Both markers achieved a diagnostic accuracy of almost 0.9 of the area under
the receiver operating characteristic curve, and the latter exhibited equivalent perform-
ance in an independent group of 62 prospectively recruited patients. Conclusion: We
developed highly accurate markers for the diagnosis of both NASH and NASH-related
ﬁbrosis (i.e., FM-NASH index and FM-ﬁbro index, respectively). These markers may be
used as an alternative diagnostic tool to liver biopsy. (HEPATOLOGY 2016;63:462-473)
N
onalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) is a
major liver disease closely associated with dia-
betes and obesity. The pathological spectrum
of NAFLD spans from nonalcoholic fatty liver (NAFL)
to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), and the latter
is considered to be as severe as liver cirrhosis, portal
hypertension, liver failure, or hepatocellular carcinoma
(HCC).1,2 Therefore, it is important that NASH
patients are diagnosed and treated early to prevent seri-
ous complications. However, current methods for
NASH diagnosis rely on invasive liver biopsy, which
makes early diagnosis difﬁcult. This encouraged us to
develop novel noninvasive markers for diagnosing
NASH.
A number of noninvasive markers for diagnosing
NASH have been reported.3,4 Although most of these

markers are designed for the pathological diagnosis of
NAFL-NASH, only three markers, that is, the NASH
test,5 NASH diagnostics,6 and NAFIC score,7 have been
conﬁrmed to have reliable diagnostic accuracy by pro-
spective validation studies. Generally, the accuracy of a
diagnostic marker can be characterized using the area
under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves
(AUROCs) for distinguishing patients from healthy
people. Accordingly, the AUROCs of the three existing
markers for training/validation data sets are 0.69/0.80,
0.91/0.70, and 0.85/0.78, respectively.5-8 All of these
markers were developed using an approach that com-
bines representing factors at each step of disease progres-
sion as pathological ﬁndings of NASH, that is, steatosis,
hepatitis (inﬂammatory inﬁltration), hepatocyte injury
(degeneration and necrosis), and liver ﬁbrosis. This
pathological approach has the obvious advantage of
exploring the optimum combination among many bio-
molecules based on training data. This advantage makes
it possible to develop markers that have low dependence
on training data and equivalent accuracy in different
groups of patients. That is, these markers have high
extrapolability to validation data. In fact, using the
NAFIC score, which has high extrapolability, a study
conﬁrmed that the difference in the AUROCs between
training and validation data is only 0.07 (0.85/0.78).7
On the other hand, the NAFLD ﬁbrosis score,9
BARD,10 and FIB-4 index11 are widely known as ﬁbro-
sis markers, which were developed for distinguishing
advanced ﬁbrosis from no/mild ﬁbrosis. However, the
accuracy of these markers in the diagnosis of mild/
advanced ﬁbrosis has not been validated in most pro-
spective studies. Thus, more accurate markers with
improved AUROCs are expected to replace liver biopsy.
In the present study, we examined the use of noninva-
sive markers in the diagnosis of NAFL-NASH and
NASH-related ﬁbrosis. We quantitatively measured 261
biomolecules from serum samples of 132 NAFLD
patients and explored the optimal markers with discrim-
inant ability for NAFL-NASH and NASH-related ﬁbro-
sis diagnoses. In addition, we adopted an approach
based on the biological events in NASH, rather than the
pathological
ﬁndings.
A
biological
event
in
this
approach
is
synonymous
with
the
so-called
“cell
function” and is annotated by a speciﬁc biological path-
way. To implement this approach, we used the concept
of “factor module,” in which multiple closely related
biomolecules were considered as one set. That is, a fac-
tor module is equivalent to one of the biological events
occurring during the course of the disease. A particular
factor module or a combination of factor modules can
be a frame alternative to the approach based on patho-
logical ﬁndings.
Materials and Methods
Patients.
A total of 132 NAFLD patients were
recruited from Saiseikai Suita Hospital in Japan and
diagnosed from July 2011 to the ﬁrst week of June
2013. For validation of marker, an independent group
of 62 NAFLD patients was prospectively recruited from
the same center and diagnosed from the second week of
June 2013 to April 2014. No patient had other hepatic
diseases caused by virus infection, autoimmune disorder,
or drug therapy, and alcohol consumption in patients
was <20 g of ethanol per day. Liver biopsy was per-
formed in all patients, and pathological diagnosis of
NAFL/NASH was made using Matteoni classiﬁcation12
by a hepatopathologist (Okanoue T.). This study was
performed in accord with the ethical guidelines of the
Declaration of Helsinki, and informed consent was
obtained from all patients before liver biopsy.
Clinical Examination.
A total of 271 items were
examined for the 132 patients. The clinical examination
of patients included six body measurements (sex, age,
height, weight, body mass index, and abdominal girth),
14 routine biochemical tests (albumin, alanine amino-
transferase [ALT], aspartate aminotransferase [AST],
fasting blood sugar, ferritin, gamma-glutamyl transpep-
tidase, glycated hemoglobin, insulin, platelets, total bili-
rubin, total cholesterol, triglyceride, type IV collagen
7S, and uric acid), and diagnosis of four concomitant
diseases (diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and
HCC). Body measurements and diagnoses of concomi-
tant diseases were performed just before liver biopsy. In
addition to the above standard clinical examination, 247
of nonroutine assay items, mainly proteins, were

DiscoveryMAP
2501 version 2.0 offered by Myriad RBM (Austin,
TX). The remaining ﬁve biomolecules, that is, hyal-
uronic acid (HA), cytokeratin 18 fragment M30 (CK-
18), procollagen-3 N-terminal peptide, Mac-2 binding
protein, and soluble CD14, which is proposed to be a
NASH diagnostic marker, were measured using quanti-
tative
determination
kits
based
on
enzyme-linked
immunosorbent assay (ELISA). The 14 of routine bio-
chemistry items and the 247 of nonroutine assay items
totaled to 261 biomolecules.
Serum samples for routine biochemical tests and bio-
molecule quantitative studies were obtained within 3
months before or after liver biopsy, except that only three
samples were around 6 months, that is, 1149, 1155,
and 2215 days from their liver biopsy. It is emphasized
that >90% of them were obtained within 1 month
(Table 1). There were missing values in 10 of the meas-
ured items. Nine of these items had missing values in
<10% of all patients. The remaining type IV collagen 7S
had missing values in approximately 20% of all patients.
Data Analysis.
The concept of “factor module,”
which was used to identify biological events in NASH,
met the following three conditions.
 Measured
items
belonging
to
a
factor
module
showed good correlation with one another.
 Measured items belonging to a factor module were
in a mutual relationship with biological regulations,
and the regulatory network reflected a step in
NAFL-NASH disease progression.
 There was low correlation among different factor
modules.
First, we identiﬁed those factor modules that fulﬁlled
the above conditions by analyzing the clinical data. The
optimum factor module or optimum combination was
then identiﬁed as a discriminant formula, which accu-
rately distinguishes NASH from NAFL. In this case, a
simple arithmetic average of all component factors that
constituted a factor module was regarded as the entire
behavior of the factor module. Finally, the discriminant
formula substituting a few representative factors for each
factor module was proposed as a novel diagnostic
marker of NAFL-NASH. A NASH-related ﬁbrosis
marker was also proposed using the same protocol.
These procedures, except for the identiﬁcation of bio-
logical regulations, were performed using the statistical
software R (version 3.1; R Foundation for Statistical
Computing, Vienna, Austria). Details regarding each
step are described as follows.
Data
Preprocessing.
To
calculate
correlations
between NASH and measured items, all categorical
data were converted to numerical data. Two-category
variables, such as histological diagnosis of NASH, sex,
hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and HCC, were con-
verted to 1/0, as applicable. Diabetes as a three-category
variable was converted to 1/0.5/0, depending on
whether diabetes was present, borderline diabetes was
present, or diabetes was absent, respectively. Moreover,
to average component factors in a factor module, all
measurements were standardized to a range from 0 to 1
after conversion to Z-scores using a standard sigmoid
function.

Extraction
of
Effective
Factors
for
Diagnosis.
Before the identiﬁcation of factor modules, effective fac-
tors comparatively correlating with disease progression
from NAFL to NASH were extracted from all measured
items. The correlation between each measured item and
disease progression was evaluated using two indicators,
that is, “state_by_measurement” (discriminant ability
for NAFL-NASH by the value of a measured item) and
“measurement_by_state”
(signiﬁcant
differences
in
measured
value
distributions
between
NAFL
and
NASH). Both indicators employed the standardized
DGini index13 as a measure. Further details are
described in Supporting Method 1. The average DGini
value for all measured items was then calculated for each
of the two indicators. Measured items having higher
DGini values than the average value for both indicators
were extracted as effective factors related to NAFL-
NASH disease progression. This bidirectional evaluation
makes it possible to rigorously evaluate the relationship
between each measured item and disease progression.
Identiﬁcation
of
Factor
Modules.
Among the
above effective factors, a set of multiple factors showing
a strong correlation was identiﬁed as a “factor module.”
The standardized DGini index, which separates the dis-
tribution of a factor by using the value of another factor,
was used to extract factor modules as an index of the
relationship between the two factors. Bidirectional
DGini indices were calculated for all combinations of
two effective factors, and the community extraction
method14 was applied to the network composed of all
effective factors and bidirectional DGini indices. The
identiﬁed “communities” were regarded as factor mod-
ules. Community extraction was performed according
to Supporting Method 2.
Factor Module Biological Annotation.
Given that
the extracted factor module is expected to reﬂect a cer-
tain biological event related to disease progression from
NAFL to NASH, we annotated these factor modules
according to the knowledge database of biological path-
ways. This annotation was performed using Pathway
Studio, offered by Elsevier (version 9.0; Mammalian
ResNet version 10.0 released June 15, 2014), which is a
commercial database consisting of pathway information
extracted by text mining from an enormous volume of
academic articles. Three types of biological information
were annotated for each factor module. One was the
regulatory relationship between factor pairs composing
a factor module, and the other two types were the path-
ological ﬁndings and cellular processes common to fac-
tors composing a factor module, respectively. Details of
these procedures are described in Supporting Method 3.
Development of a Factor Module-Based Diagnos-
tic Formula.
Because the extracted factor modules
were independent, and each reﬂected a certain biological
event related to disease progression from NAFL to
NASH, a combination of the selected factor modules
was expected to be a good marker for diagnosing
NAFL-NASH. Therefore, we deﬁned the average values
of the standardized scores of all factors composing a fac-
tor module as the scores representing the entire behavior
of the factor module. To preprocess this average calcula-
tion, the raw measured value of a factor was applied
using the standard sigmoid function after being con-
verted to a Z-score. If the average value in NASH
patients was lower than that in NAFL patients, the value
was multiplied by -1. The average score ( 

Accuracy of a Representative Factor-Based Diag-
nostic Formula.
In order to identify representative
factors of a factor module, the correlation between the
average score of the factor module and that of one or
two factors composing the factor module was calculated
according to Pearson’s correlation coefﬁcient. Factor sin-
gles and pairs were listed when their R-squared values
were >0.7. Representative factors were then selected
from this list based on the robust representative ability
of the factor module. Finally, the average value of the
standardized scores calculated from the representative
factors was assigned to the diagnostic formula that was

Results
Patient Statistics for Disease Progression
Statistics of physical features and comorbidities in the
study patients are summarized in Table 1. Statistics of
261 biomolecules are described in Supporting Table 1.
Of the 132 NAFLD patients, 91 were pathologically
diagnosed with NASH (Matteoni type 3 or 4), and 41
were diagnosed with NAFL (Matteoni type 1 or 2). All
patients with Matteoni type 4 had liver ﬁbrosis. The
average of body mass index in all Matteoni types was
<30, indicating that there was no disproportionate
weight distribution among extremely obese patients.
The four types of concomitant diseases did not tend to
closely correlate with NASH disease progression, except
for diabetes. The proportion of patients with diabetes
was speciﬁcally high among those with Matteoni type 3.
Effective Factors for Diagnosis
First, we calculated two types of indicators (standardized
DGini indexes), that is, “measurement_ by_state” and
“state_by_measurement.” The average values of these
standardized DGini
indexes
in
NAFL
and
NASH
patients were 0.0380 for “measurement_by_state” and
0.0578 for “state_by_measurement.” A total of 70 meas-
ured items (about 26%) with higher-than-average values
for both DGini indexes were extracted as the effective
factors
related
to
NAFL-NASH
disease
progression
(Supporting Fig. 1). The extracted factors included ﬁve
kinds of routine biochemistry items (albumin, ALT,
AST, insulin, and type IV collagen 7S) and 65 nonrou-
tine assay items.
Factor Modules
Community extraction for the network consisting of
effective factors and their mutual discriminant ability
resulted in four kinds of factor modules, that is, M1-M4
(Table 2). All of these factor modules were composed of
16-18 factors (measured items), as well as all effective
factors belonged to any of these factor modules. Of the
effective factors, two interleukins (interleukin-1 beta
and interleukin-23) and 2 apoproteins (apolipoprotein
C-III and apolipoprotein D) were considered as M1,
whereas type IV collagen 7S and type IV collagen, which
are actually the same protein measured using different
methods, were classiﬁed as M2. M3 contained three
transaminases (ALT, AST, and phosphoserine amino-
transferase), and M4 contained 10 growth factors (e.g.,
transforming growth factor alpha and basic ﬁbroblast
growth factor). These results indicate that the factor
modules identiﬁed by community extraction have strong
inside relationships and weak outside relationships.
Thus, these modules are satisﬁed with two of three con-
ditions for factor-module described in the Data Analysis
section of Materials and Methods.

Diagnostic Marker for NAFL-NASH
Diagnostic Formula for NAFL-NASH Based on Fac-
tor Modules.
Each of the factor modules identiﬁed by
community extraction and biological annotation can be
regarded as an index for the biological events related to
NAFL-NASH disease progression. Thus, the combina-
tion of two or more factor modules is expected to be a
good diagnostic marker of NAFL-NASH. Before deter-
mining the optimum combination of factor modules,
we evaluated the discriminant ability of each factor
module to NAFL-NASH. All AUROCs of M1-M4
were >0.8 and those of M1 (0.832) and M3 (0.846)
were comparatively high. These values are almost as
high as the NAFIC score (0.85/0.78), which shows the
best value of AUROC for validation tests among the
known markers. Moreover, the AUROC of the NAFIC
score was 0.834 in a part of the data set of this study,
which comprised only 97 patients with available items
(ferritin, insulin, and type IV collagen 7S). Next, com-
putation of logistic regression analysis using any pairs
of the factor modules as variables revealed a regression
formula for M1 and M3, with the highest AUROC of
0.939 (Table 4). This value is far higher than that
obtained using M1 and M3 separately and is therefore
enough to alter liver biopsy. Actually, the difference of
the AUROCs was conﬁrmed to be statistically signiﬁ-
cant (P < 0.01) by a t test. Logistic regression analysis
using all factor modules as variables resulted in an
AUROC of 0.946, which was almost equivalent to that
of the M1 and M3 pair. Thus, we conclude that the
optimal diagnostic formula is the combination of M1
and M3. Supporting Table 2 summarizes the average
values and standard deviation among patients for each
factor. These values are necessary to calculate the aver-
age score of a factor module.
Representative Factors for M1 and M3.
The
regression formula consisting of M1 and M3 as men-
tioned above would provide a highly accurate diagnostic
marker for NAFL-NASH, if all the factors composing
M1 and M3 are easily measured. However, markers
with fewer measured items are expected in clinical set-
tings, because these reduce measurement costs and
require fewer blood samples. Therefore, we investigated
a limited number of representative factors that could
detect the entire behavior of a factor module. Basically,
each of the factors composing a factor module was
thought to be a possible representative factor, because all
factors mutually correlated. However, it is believed that
the expected representative factors should have high cor-
relation with the entire behavior of the factor module
and adequate robustness for measurement errors and

Accuracy of NAFL-NASH Diagnosis Using Repre-
sentative
Factors.
We evaluated the accuracy of
NAFL-NASH diagnosis by using the M1 and M3 repre-
sentative factors in the diagnostic formula (Table 6).
When four factors including two for M1 and M3 each
were used, the AUROC scores were approximately 0.9
(0.889-0.904). Moreover, when ﬁve factors including
two for M1 and three for M3 were used, the AUROCs
were around 0.9 (0.902-0.915). In this calculation, the
coefﬁcients of M1 and M3 used in the diagnostic for-
mula were not derived from the logistic regression analy-
sis for the scores of the representative factors, but from
the average scores of the module factors. Thus, the
AUROC is a highly reliable measure, and equivalent
accuracy would be expected in different patient groups.
Hence, the identiﬁed diagnostic formulas comprising
four to ﬁve factors are expected to be good diagnostic
markers of NAFL-NASH.
Diagnostic Marker for NASH-Related Fibrosis
M2 as a Potential NASH-Related Fibrosis Marker.
Among the four factor modules identiﬁed in this study,
M2 and M4 were not adopted as diagnostic markers for
NAFL-NASH. Given that the annotation described in
Table 3 shows that both M2 and M4 are strongly related
to hepatocyte injury and/or liver ﬁbrosis, it is suggested
that M2 and M4 help in distinguishing NASH-related
ﬁbrosis from NAFLD. Thus, we calculated the accuracy
of differentiating Matteoni type 4 from types 1 to 3 by
using each of these module factors. As in the case of dis-
tinguishing NASH from NAFL, AUROCs were calcu-
lated using the average values of the standardized scores
derived from all factors composing a factor module. As a
result, the AUROC of M4 was at most 0.798, whereas
that of M2 had high accuracy at 0.867 (Table 7). More-
over, when advanced ﬁbrosis was evaluated using the
ﬁbrosis stage,16 which is a histological indicator of
NASH-related ﬁbrosis, the AUROC of M2 showed very
high
accuracy
(>0.9)
for
differentiating
between
advanced ﬁbrosis (ﬁbrosis stages 3-4) and no/mild ﬁbrosis
(ﬁbrosis stages 0-2; Table 7). Existing ﬁbrosis markers
(NAFLD ﬁbrosis score,9 BARD,10 and FIB-4 index11)
have been validated in one or more prospective studies,
and their AUROCs were reported to be 0.64-0.85, 0.67-
0.82, and 0.80-0.87, respectively.7,9,10,17-19 When exist-
ing ﬁbrosis markers were used in this study, their
AUROCs were within the reported values (0.761, 0.698,
and 0.853, respectively). Hence, M2 is expected to be a
NASH-related ﬁbrosis marker with a higher accuracy
than the existing markers. Moreover, M2 is thought to be
an ideal diagnostic marker for monitoring NAFL, NASH
without ﬁbrosis, and NASH with ﬁbrosis.

Similar to the process used for the diagnos-

Biological Annotation of Diagnostic Markers.
The
enrichment score proﬁles for the four pathological ﬁnd-
ings in NAFL-NASH (steatosis, hepatitis, hepatocyte
injury, and liver ﬁbrosis) suggest that the four factor
modules include diverse biological events that occur
during disease progression from NAFL to NASH (Table
3). Before analysis, we expected the optimum combina-
tion to be M2 and M3, because NASH could be distin-
guished from NAFL by progression from hepatitis to
hepatocyte injury. However, the M1 and M3 combina-
tion showed the highest accuracy for diagnosing NAFL-
NASH. It is interesting that the optimal combination
includes M1 associated with no pathological ﬁndings
and M3 associated with hepatitis. It is not completely
clear as to why a combination of these two biological
events is the best diagnostic indicator for NAFL-NASH,
but it is certain that this combination has the potential
to be a better marker than the existing ones.
Biological Role of Representative Factors in Each
Factor Module.
We revealed the biological roles of
each factor module (Table 3). Here, we considered the
biological role of representative factors in each factor
module. Of three representative factors for M2 consti-
tuting the FM-ﬁbro index, HA was located upstream in
the regulatory network of M2, and COL4-7S and
VCAM-1 were downstream (Table 3). According to the
pathway in the commercial database, COL4-7 is known
to regulate “cell-cell adhesion,” and VCAM-1 regulates
the remaining cellular processes. However, of two repre-
sentative factors for M1 composing the FM-NASH
index, PROS1 regulates a network of growth hormones
in connection with a protective response to hepatic stea-
tosis, and CLU is regulated by a network of them. For
M3, all combinations of representative factors included
AST. AST is a well-known tissue damage marker of
inﬂammation and actually located the most downstream
(Table 3). LEP and ICAM1, which were the other repre-
sentative factors in combination with AST, developed a
complicate
regulatory
network
with
some
known
NASH-related markers (e.g., AST, C-reactive protein,
and insulin). The combination of representative factors
expands the coverage on the regulatory network of each
factor module.
Effect of Missing Values on Diagnostic Marker
Development.
Of 271 measured items in this study,
only 10 items had unmeasured values. These missing val-
ues can have serious effects on the reliability of the identi-
ﬁed markers in some cases. However, our diagnostic
formulas were developed using the average values of all
factors composing a factor module as a variable, and
therefore the inﬂuence was exceedingly small. For exam-
ple, COL4-7S, which had the highest number of missing
values, was correlated with 17 of the other factors in M2,
and M2 included type IV collagen for which the same
protein was measured by using a different method. Thus,
the missing values in COL4-7S had an insigniﬁcant effect
on the calculation of the average score of M2. By using
COL4-7S as a constitutive factor for the FM-ﬁbro index,
the performance of validation data on the 62 patients was
conﬁrmed to be as high as that on the exploratory patient
group. We emphasize that there is no missing value for
COL4-7S in the validation data set.
Use of Standardized Scores in Diagnostic Formu-
las.
Whereas existing diagnostic markers have been
designed using each measured item independently, we
introduced a novel concept of “factor module” where
multiple mutually correlated measured items were con-
sidered as one set. This concept requires the use of com-
parable standardized scores, which can equivalently and
mutually be compared with other factors, rather than
raw measured values. The use of standardized scores is
thought to provide additional value to the diagnostic
formula. That is, we can easily develop diagnostic
markers optimized to a speciﬁc region or race not by
changing the formula but by substituting the mean and
standard deviation values. In addition, it is noteworthy
that the mean and standard deviation values depend on
the patient population. For instance, the prevalence of
NASH in the NAFLD American population is esti-
mated to be approximately 20%,20,21 whereas it is
>50% in most marker studies including the present
study.
Thus,
it
is
preferable
to
use
population-
independent
mean and standard deviation
values.
Therefore, we introduced another method to calculate
mean and standard deviation values by considering the
NAFL/NASH ratio as equal. In this method, mean and
standard deviation values were calculated after weighing
by the inverse number of NAFL/NASH patients. Thus,
we validated the diagnostic accuracy of the markers by
using this population-independent value.
Perspective of FM-NASH Index and FM-Fibro
Index.
To evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and extrap-
olability of the markers, it is necessary to perform a
study with a large number of patients recruited from
multiple clinical centers. Currently, we are planning a
large-scale external validation study for the FM-ﬁbro
index. On the other hand, the FM-NASH index could
not be validated even in a small number of patients.
However, the FM-NASH index is expected to show
high performance, similar to the FM-ﬁbro index,
because these markers were identiﬁed using the same
approach. Therefore, future studies should be performed
to establish quantitative measurements for PROS1 and
